changes.before: If VERBOSE is defined as 1, which text prints?
changes.after: Conditional compilation chooses which code is included before the program is built.

before:
#if examines integer preprocessing expressions. A -D flag can define a configuration macro; #ifndef supplies a default only when the build did not define it. Code in an excluded branch is not compiled as C.

For the complete source below saved as main.c, this terminal command supplies the macro before preprocessing:
```sh
gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -DVERBOSE=1 main.c -o app
./app
```
On Linux or macOS, running that executable prints details. The command assumes GCC is already installed.

Use documented feature macros to check optional facilities rather than guessing from an operating-system name. This tiny configuration chooses text; it is not proof that every C23 feature is implemented. The course uses C17 on GCC14.2.
Expected output or behavior: brief. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Compile with -DVERBOSE=1 instead of editing the default and explain why the guard preserves the build choice. You may trace it without a C compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: Preprocessing is the step that handles directives such as `#if` before C compilation. `#ifndef VERBOSE` means use the following default only if VERBOSE is not already defined. `#if VERBOSE` then chooses one branch using its integer value.

Conditional compilation can also handle optional features. Use a compiler's documented feature checks instead of assuming every operating system offers the same tools. This example only chooses a message; the course uses C17 rules.
With no build setting, VERBOSE becomes 0. The selected MESSAGE is brief, so the program prints brief. The other branch does not run later; it was left out before compilation.

With GCC, add `-DVERBOSE=1` to the build command. For example, use `gcc -std=c17 -Wall -Wextra -Wpedantic -Werror -DVERBOSE=1 main.c -o app`. The default guard preserves this setting, and the new program prints details.
